about: Big Issues in Economics and Finance (BUSI40004) is a 5-ECTS compulsory Year 1 module in Imperial Business School's BSc Economics, Finance and Data Science, taught in the Autumn term according to the 2024-25 programme specification. Imperial does not publish a syllabus. A student blog on the Business School site (March 2025, about the writer's first term in 2024-25) says each lecture takes a key contemporary issue in economics and finance, explains the key models rigorously and links them to recent developments. The topics here are not an official list: they are built from that description and the programme's stated themes (the big issues of our time, such as climate change, global inequality and economic development), so the issues covered in your year may differ; check them against your lecture list. No module-level assessment breakdown is published.
topics: Climate change: externalities and carbon pricing

notes.body:
Inflation is the rate at which the general price level rises. In the UK it is measured mainly by the Consumer Prices Index (CPI), published monthly by the Office for National Statistics. CPI inflation peaked at 11.1% in October 2022, its highest rate for about 40 years, so how inflation arises and how central banks respond is a natural "big issue". A 2025 student blog about the programme's first term also mentions a guest lecture on the importance of expectations in combating inflation, though it does not say which module it belonged to.

Why inflation matters
- It erodes the real value of money, wages and savings, redistributing from lenders to borrowers when it is unexpected.
- High and variable inflation makes relative prices harder to read and complicates long-term contracts and investment.
- Very low inflation or deflation can also be harmful because nominal interest rates cannot easily go far below zero.

Causes
- Demand-pull: aggregate demand grows faster than the economy's capacity.
- Cost-push: supply shocks such as energy prices raise costs (as after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022).
- Expectations: if firms and workers expect high inflation, they set prices and wages accordingly, which makes it self-fulfilling.
- Quantity theory: MV = PY, so with stable velocity V, sustained money growth beyond real output growth Y shows up as inflation.

The Phillips curve and expectations
A. W. Phillips (1958) found a negative relationship between UK unemployment and wage inflation. Milton Friedman (1968) and Edmund Phelps (1967) argued that any trade-off is only temporary because people adapt their expectations. The expectations-augmented Phillips curve is:

π = πᵉ − β(u − u*)

where πᵉ is expected inflation and u* is the natural rate of unemployment. Example: with πᵉ = 2%, β = 0.5, u = 3% and u* = 4%, inflation is 2 + 0.5 = 2.5%. Holding unemployment below u* only raises inflation further as expectations catch up, so in the long run the curve is vertical at u*.

Monetary policy in the UK
- The Bank of England has had operational independence over interest rates since 1997 (put on a statutory footing by the Bank of England Act 1998).
- The Chancellor sets a CPI inflation target of 2%; the nine-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) sets Bank Rate to meet it.
- Bank Rate was raised from 0.1% (the first rise came in December 2021) to 5.25% in August 2023, the fastest tightening for decades.
- Transmission: higher rates raise borrowing costs, reduce spending and asset prices, strengthen the exchange rate and, crucially, signal commitment, which anchors expectations.

Credibility and rules
If the central bank is credible, expectations stay anchored near target, so shocks fade with less unemployment cost. The Taylor rule (1993) summarises a sensible response:
i = r* + π + 0.5(π − π*) + 0.5(output gap)
With r* = 1%, π = 4%, π* = 2% and an output gap of −1%: i = 1 + 4 + 1 − 0.5 = 5.5%. Because the coefficient on inflation is greater than one in total, the real interest rate rises when inflation rises.

The Fisher relation links nominal and real rates: real rate ≈ nominal rate − expected inflation (5% − 3% ≈ 2%; exactly 1.05/1.03 − 1 ≈ 1.94%).

Exam tips: distinguish demand-pull from cost-push, explain why expectations make the long-run Phillips curve vertical, and use real interest rates when judging how tight policy is.

notes.h: Climate change: externalities and carbon pricing
notes.body:
Climate change is one of the issues the programme highlights. Economists treat it as the largest example of an externality: the costs of greenhouse gas emissions fall on people around the world and in the future, not on the emitter. Nicholas Stern's 2006 review for the UK Treasury called it the greatest market failure the world has seen.

Externalities
- A negative externality is a cost imposed on third parties that is not reflected in the price. The private marginal cost (MPC) is below the social marginal cost (MSC = MPC + marginal external cost).
- Markets therefore produce too much of the polluting good: output is set where demand equals MPC rather than MSC.
- Arthur Pigou (The Economics of Welfare, 1920) proposed a tax equal to the marginal external cost at the optimum: a Pigouvian tax.

Worked example
Demand: P = 100 − Q. Private marginal cost: MPC = 20 + Q. Each unit causes £20 of external damage, so MSC = 40 + Q.
- Market outcome: 100 − Q = 20 + Q gives Q = 40 and P = 60.
- Social optimum: 100 − Q = 40 + Q gives Q = 30 and P = 70.
- Deadweight loss of the market outcome: ½ × (40 − 30) × 20 = 100.
- A tax of £20 per unit makes producers face the full social cost, moving output to 30.

Carbon pricing tools
- Carbon tax: sets the price of emissions and lets the quantity adjust. Predictable for firms, raises revenue, but the eventual emissions level is uncertain.
- Cap-and-trade (emissions trading): sets the quantity of permits and lets the market find the price. Certain about total emissions, but the carbon price can be volatile. Examples: the EU Emissions Trading System (from 2005) and the UK ETS (from 1 January 2021).
- Martin Weitzman's "Prices vs. Quantities" (1974) shows the choice depends on how steep the marginal damage and marginal abatement cost curves are when costs are uncertain.
- Both approaches achieve a given cut at the lowest total cost because firms with cheap abatement cut most (equalising marginal abatement costs), unlike uniform regulation.

Coase and bargaining
Ronald Coase ("The Problem of Social Cost", 1960) showed that if property rights are clear and bargaining is costless, private negotiation can reach an efficient outcome. For climate change, with billions of affected people and future generations, transaction costs make this unrealistic.

Global public good and free-riding
Emissions reductions benefit everyone, whoever pays, so each country has an incentive to free-ride. International agreements such as the Paris Agreement (2015), which aims to keep warming well below 2°C and pursue 1.5°C, rely on nationally determined contributions rather than binding enforcement. Carbon border adjustments (the EU's CBAM is being phased in) try to reduce "carbon leakage" to countries with weaker policies.

Discounting
Climate damage happens far in the future, so the discount rate is crucial. Stern used a very low pure rate of time preference, justifying rapid action. William Nordhaus, whose integrated assessment (DICE) models earned a share of the 2018 Nobel Prize, used market-based rates that favoured a more gradual policy ramp. The social cost of carbon (the present value of damage from one extra tonne of CO₂) is highly sensitive to this choice.

UK policy
The Climate Change Act 2008 created legally binding carbon budgets and the independent Climate Change Committee; a 2019 amendment set a target of net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.

Exam tips: draw the externality diagram with MPC, MSC and demand, label the deadweight loss triangle, and evaluate taxes versus permits rather than just describing them.

Inequality of income and wealth is one of the programme's highlighted big issues. You need to be able to measure it, explain what drives it and evaluate what policy can do.

Income versus wealth
- Income is a flow (wages, profits, interest, transfers over a period).
- Wealth is a stock (housing, pensions, financial assets, minus debts). Wealth is far more unequally distributed than income in the UK and most rich countries.
- Inequality can be measured before taxes and benefits (market income) or after (disposable income); the gap shows how much redistribution occurs.

Measuring inequality
- Lorenz curve: plots the cumulative share of income against the cumulative share of the population, from poorest to richest. Perfect equality is the 45° line.
- Gini coefficient: the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve divided by the whole area under the line of equality. It runs from 0 (everyone has the same) to 1 (one person has everything).
- Share-based measures: the top 1% or top 10% share; the Palma ratio (income share of the top 10% divided by that of the bottom 40%); the 90/10 ratio.
- Each measure is sensitive to different parts of the distribution: the Gini is most sensitive to changes around the middle; top shares capture the very rich.

Worked example
Five people have incomes 10, 20, 30, 40 and 100 (total 200, mean 40).
- Gini = sum of all absolute differences between pairs ÷ (2n² × mean) = 800 ÷ (2 × 25 × 40) = 0.40.
- The richest person (top 20%) receives 100/200 = 50% of income; the poorest two (bottom 40%) receive 30/200 = 15%.

Causes of rising inequality since 1980 in many rich countries
- Skill-biased technological change: computers and automation raised demand for highly educated workers. Claudia Goldin and Lawrence Katz (The Race between Education and Technology, 2008) argue wages depend on whether the supply of skills keeps up.
- Globalisation: trade and offshoring put pressure on lower-skilled manufacturing wages in rich countries while lifting incomes in emerging economies. Branko Milanović's "elephant curve" shows strong income growth for the global middle and the very top, and weak growth for the lower-middle classes of rich countries, over roughly 1988 to 2008.
- Institutions: declining union membership, lower top tax rates and changes in pay-setting norms for executives.
- Superstar firms and winner-take-all markets (see the market power topic).
- Returns to capital: Thomas Piketty (Capital in the Twenty-First Century, 2013) argued that when the return on capital r exceeds growth g, inherited wealth tends to grow relative to income, concentrating wealth.

Theories of inequality and growth
- Simon Kuznets (1955) suggested inequality first rises then falls as economies industrialise (the Kuznets curve). Post-1980 rises in rich countries challenge this.
- Arthur Okun (1975) described an equality-efficiency "big tradeoff": redistribution can weaken incentives, like carrying water in a leaky bucket.
- Others argue high inequality can harm growth by limiting investment in education by poorer families, and the "Great Gatsby curve" links higher inequality with lower intergenerational mobility across countries.

Policy options
- Progressive income taxes and means-tested benefits (redistribution).
- Wealth, inheritance and property taxation.
- Minimum wages (the UK National Living Wage) and support for collective bargaining.
- "Predistribution": education, early-years support and skills policy to change market incomes before tax.
Each involves trade-offs between equity, efficiency, administrative feasibility and political support.

Exam tips: define your measure before using it, be careful to separate income from wealth, and link causes to evidence and named authors with dates.

Over long periods, living standards depend almost entirely on productivity growth. The programme lists innovation-led growth among its big themes, and the 2025 Nobel Prize in Economics went to Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt for explaining innovation-driven economic growth.

The power of compounding
- Rule of 70: a variable growing at g% a year doubles in about 70 ÷ g years. At 2% a year, income doubles in about 35 years; at 1%, about 70.
- Small differences in growth rates, sustained, produce large differences in living standards.

The Solow model (Robert Solow, 1956)
- Output Y = F(K, AL), with diminishing returns to capital.
- Capital per worker k evolves as Δk = s f(k) − (n + δ)k, where s is the saving rate, n population growth and δ depreciation.
- In the steady state, investment just offsets depreciation and dilution: s f(k*) = (n + δ)k*.
- Example: f(k) = k^0.5, s = 0.2, n = 0.01, δ = 0.05. Then k* = (s/(n + δ))² = (0.2/0.06)² ≈ 11.1, output per worker y* = √11.1 ≈ 3.33 and consumption per worker (1 − s)y* ≈ 2.67.
- Key result: higher saving raises the level of income but not its long-run growth rate. Sustained growth in income per head requires continuing technological progress (growth in A), which the basic model takes as given (exogenous).
- Conditional convergence: poorer countries with similar fundamentals should grow faster as they catch up.

Growth accounting
With a Cobb-Douglas function Y = A K^α L^(1−α):
g_Y = g_A + α g_K + (1 − α) g_L
Total factor productivity (TFP) growth is the residual. Example: output grows 3%, capital 4%, labour 1%, α = 0.3: g_A = 3 − 1.2 − 0.7 = 1.1%.

Endogenous growth
- Paul Romer (1990) modelled ideas as non-rival: once discovered they can be used by everyone at once, giving increasing returns. Investment in research, driven by the prospect of temporary monopoly profits, generates growth from within the model. Romer shared the 2018 Nobel Prize.
- Aghion and Howitt (1992) formalised Joseph Schumpeter's "creative destruction" (Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy, 1942): new innovations displace old firms and products. Growth depends on competition, patent protection and the threat of entry, and the relationship between competition and innovation can be an inverted U.
- Mokyr's historical work stresses the culture of useful knowledge and science that made sustained innovation possible from the Industrial Revolution onwards.

The productivity puzzle
- UK labour productivity growth has been much weaker since the 2008 financial crisis than in the preceding decades, one of the worst records in the G7.
- Possible explanations: weak investment, misallocation of credit to low-productivity "zombie" firms, slower diffusion of technology from leading to lagging firms, and mismeasurement.
- Intangibles: Jonathan Haskel and Stian Westlake (Capitalism without Capital, 2017) argue modern investment is increasingly in software, data, design and brands, which scale easily, create spillovers and are hard to borrow against, and may help explain both weak measured investment and rising gaps between firms.
- Solow's 1987 paradox ("You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics") is now asked about AI.

Exam tips: show the Solow steady-state condition and explain why saving cannot drive permanent growth, compute a growth-accounting residual, and connect theory to the UK productivity slowdown.

The 2007-09 global financial crisis showed how problems in the financial system can cause deep recessions. Understanding why banks are fragile and how regulators try to make them safer is central to any course on big issues in finance.

Why banks are fragile
- Maturity transformation: banks fund long-term, illiquid loans (such as mortgages) with short-term deposits that can be withdrawn on demand.
- Bank runs: Douglas Diamond and Philip Dybvig (1983) showed that this structure creates two equilibria. If depositors expect others to withdraw, it is rational for each to withdraw too, and even a solvent bank can fail. Diamond, Dybvig and Ben Bernanke shared the 2022 Nobel Prize.
- Leverage: banks hold little equity relative to assets. With assets of 100 and equity of 5, leverage is 20; a 5% fall in asset values wipes out the equity. High leverage also magnifies returns: if assets earn 1% after funding costs, return on equity is 20%.
- Interconnectedness: banks lend to each other and hold similar assets, so one failure can spread through fire sales and counterparty losses (contagion).

The 2007-09 crisis
- A US housing boom was fuelled by lending to riskier (subprime) borrowers. Mortgages were packaged into complex securities rated as safe and held across the global system.
- When house prices fell, losses on these assets and uncertainty about who held them froze wholesale funding markets.
- In the UK, Northern Rock, which relied heavily on wholesale funding, suffered the first British bank run for well over a century in September 2007.
- Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on 15 September 2008, triggering panic. Governments recapitalised banks, central banks cut rates to near zero and began quantitative easing.

Theories of crises
- Hyman Minsky's financial instability hypothesis: long periods of stability encourage riskier borrowing, moving from "hedge" to "speculative" to "Ponzi" finance, until a "Minsky moment" when asset prices fall.
- Charles Kindleberger (Manias, Panics, and Crashes, 1978) documented repeated patterns of credit-fuelled booms and busts.
- Walter Bagehot (Lombard Street, 1873) set out the lender-of-last-resort principle: in a panic, lend freely to solvent institutions against good collateral at a penalty rate.

Regulatory responses
- Basel III (agreed from 2010): more and better-quality capital, a leverage ratio, and liquidity rules such as the Liquidity Coverage Ratio.
- Macroprudential policy: the Bank of England's Financial Policy Committee monitors system-wide risk and can, for example, set the countercyclical capital buffer.
- Ring-fencing (from 2019, following the Vickers Independent Commission on Banking): large UK banks must separate core retail banking from riskier investment banking.
- Resolution regimes and "bail-in" debt aim to let banks fail without taxpayer bailouts, reducing the moral hazard created by "too big to fail".

More recent episodes
- In September 2022, a sharp rise in gilt yields after the UK government's fiscal statement forced pension funds using liability-driven investment (LDI) strategies to sell gilts to meet collateral calls, and the Bank of England intervened with temporary gilt purchases.
- In March 2023, Silicon Valley Bank in the US failed after losses on long-dated bonds and a rapid, social-media-accelerated deposit run, showing that interest-rate risk and run dynamics remain relevant.

Exam tips: explain mechanisms (maturity mismatch, leverage, contagion) rather than narrating events, use a numerical leverage example, and evaluate whether reforms address moral hazard and runs.

How markets evolve, and whether a few dominant firms are gaining too much power, is a live debate in economics and finance. Questions about digital platforms, "superstar" firms and competition policy connect microeconomic theory to the big issues of inequality and growth.

Market power and its costs
- A firm has market power when it can set price above marginal cost without losing all its customers.
- A profit-maximising monopolist sets marginal revenue equal to marginal cost, producing less and charging more than under perfect competition.
- Worked example: demand P = 100 − Q, constant marginal cost 20. Under perfect competition P = MC, so Q = 80 and P = 20. A monopolist sets MR = 100 − 2Q = 20, so Q = 40 and P = 60. Profit = (60 − 20) × 40 = 1,600. Consumer surplus falls from 3,200 to 800, and the deadweight loss is ½ × (80 − 40) × (60 − 20) = 800.

Measuring market power
- Lerner index: L = (P − MC) ÷ P. For a profit-maximising firm, L = 1 ÷ |price elasticity of demand|. With elasticity −4, L = 0.25, so P = MC ÷ (1 − 0.25); if MC is £30, P = £40.
- Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI): the sum of squared market shares (in percentages). Shares of 40, 30, 20 and 10 give 1,600 + 900 + 400 + 100 = 3,000. Higher values mean a more concentrated market; a monopoly scores 10,000.
- Concentration ratios: the combined share of the largest few firms (e.g. CR4).

Evidence of rising market power
- Jan De Loecker, Jan Eeckhout and Gabriel Unger (Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2020) estimate that aggregate (sales-weighted average) markups of US listed firms rose from 21% above marginal cost in 1980 to 61% by 2016. The median markup barely changed: the rise came mainly from firms in the upper tail of the distribution and from market share shifting towards high-markup firms.
- David Autor and co-authors (2020) link rising concentration to "superstar firms" that win most of their markets, which may help explain the falling share of national income paid to labour.
- Critics argue that higher markups may reflect higher fixed costs (such as software and R&D) rather than weaker competition, so welfare conclusions are debated.

Why digital markets are different
- Network effects: a platform becomes more valuable as more people use it, so markets can "tip" to one winner.
- Economies of scale and scope in data, very low marginal costs, and the ability to self-preference on platforms the firm itself runs.
- Zero monetary prices make traditional price-based tests of harm harder to apply.

Competition policy in the UK
- The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) enforces the Competition Act 1998: Chapter I prohibits anti-competitive agreements (such as cartels) and Chapter II prohibits abuse of a dominant position.
- The CMA reviews mergers under the Enterprise Act 2002 and can block or impose remedies on deals that substantially lessen competition.
- The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 lets the CMA designate firms with "strategic market status" in digital activities and impose tailored conduct requirements.

Static versus dynamic efficiency
Market power causes static deadweight losses, but the prospect of monopoly profits also funds innovation (as in Schumpeterian growth theory). Good policy aims to protect the process of competition, including entry by challengers, rather than simply penalising size.

Exam tips: be ready to calculate monopoly price, output and deadweight loss, compute the Lerner index and HHI, and evaluate evidence on markups with its caveats.

questions.q: Using π = πᵉ − β(u − u*), with expected inflation 3%, β = 0.5, unemployment 6% and natural rate 4%, what is inflation?
questions.why: π = 3 − 0.5 × (6 − 4) = 3 − 1 = 2%. 4% adds the unemployment term instead of subtracting it, 3% ignores the gap between u and u*, and 1% doubles the gap effect by leaving out β.

questions.q: Why does a credible inflation-targeting central bank make it less costly to bring inflation down?
options: Because expectations stay anchored, so wage and price setting adjusts quickly without a long period of high unemployment
Because credibility lets the bank set real interest rates permanently below zero
Because a credible bank can print money without causing inflation
Because credibility removes supply shocks such as energy price rises
questions.why: If people believe inflation will return to target, they build lower inflation into wages and prices, so less slack is needed to reduce it. Credibility does not allow permanently negative real rates without consequences, does not cancel the link between excessive money growth and inflation, and cannot stop external supply shocks.

questions.q: Using the expectations-augmented Phillips curve, explain why a government that tries to keep unemployment permanently below the natural rate will end up with rising inflation.
markScheme: States π = πᵉ − β(u − u*) and defines terms
Short run: with expectations fixed, u below u* raises inflation above expected
Expectations adapt upwards (πᵉ rises to match actual inflation)
To keep u below u*, inflation must keep exceeding the new higher expectations, so inflation accelerates
Long-run Phillips curve vertical at u*: no permanent trade-off (Friedman 1968, Phelps 1967)
questions.modelAnswer: The expectations-augmented Phillips curve is π = πᵉ − β(u − u*), where u* is the natural rate. Suppose expected inflation is 2% and the government stimulates demand to push unemployment below u*. In the short run, with expectations fixed, inflation rises above 2%. Workers and firms then revise their expectations upwards, so πᵉ rises, and the short-run curve shifts up. To hold unemployment below u* the government must now generate inflation above this higher expected rate, and so on: inflation keeps accelerating. The only unemployment rate consistent with stable inflation is u*, so the long-run Phillips curve is vertical, as Friedman and Phelps argued in the late 1960s, a prediction borne out by the stagflation of the 1970s.

questions.q: Demand is P = 100 − Q, private marginal cost is 20 + Q and the external cost is £20 per unit. What is the socially optimal output?
questions.why: Social marginal cost is 40 + Q; setting 100 − Q = 40 + Q gives Q = 30. 40 is the unregulated market output where demand meets private cost, 20 is the external cost per unit rather than a quantity, and 70 is the price at the social optimum (100 − 30), not the quantity.

questions.q: Why do economists usually prefer carbon pricing to requiring every firm to cut emissions by the same percentage?
options: Pricing lets firms with cheap abatement cut more, so a given total reduction is achieved at lower cost
Pricing guarantees a specific total level of emissions under every scheme
Uniform cuts would raise government revenue whereas pricing does not
Pricing removes the free-rider problem between countries
questions.why: With a common price each firm abates until its marginal cost equals the price, equalising marginal abatement costs, which minimises total cost. A carbon tax does not guarantee the emissions level (only a cap does), uniform mandates raise no revenue while taxes and auctioned permits do, and pricing in one country does not stop others free-riding.

questions.q: Compare a carbon tax with a cap-and-trade scheme as ways of reducing emissions. Which would you recommend for the UK, and why?
markScheme: Both internalise the externality and equalise marginal abatement costs (cost-effective)
Tax: price certainty, revenue, but emissions uncertain
Cap-and-trade: quantity certainty (fits legally binding carbon budgets), but volatile prices; free allocation may weaken incentives or create windfalls
Weitzman (1974): relative slopes of marginal damage and abatement cost under uncertainty
Reasoned recommendation, e.g. cap-and-trade with a price floor/ceiling (hybrid), referring to UK ETS and carbon budgets
Mentions distributional effects or carbon leakage and use of revenue
questions.modelAnswer: Both instruments put a price on carbon so that each emitter cuts until its marginal abatement cost equals that price, which achieves any given reduction at least cost. A carbon tax fixes the price: firms can plan investment, and the revenue can be recycled to compensate poorer households, but the emissions outcome is uncertain. Cap-and-trade fixes the quantity, which matches the UK's legally binding carbon budgets under the Climate Change Act 2008, but the permit price can swing with the economy, discouraging long-term investment, and free allocation of permits can blunt incentives or give windfall profits. Weitzman's analysis suggests that because climate damage depends on the cumulative stock of emissions, the marginal damage of any one year's emissions is fairly flat, which favours price instruments in the short run. I would recommend keeping the UK ETS for heavy industry and power, because it fits the carbon budgets and the UK and EU agreed in 2025 to work towards linking it with the EU ETS, but with a price floor and ceiling to reduce volatility, and extending carbon pricing to other sectors, with revenue used to offset regressive effects on households.

questions.q: Five people have incomes of 10, 20, 30, 40 and 100. What is the Gini coefficient (using mean absolute difference ÷ twice the mean)?
questions.why: The sum of absolute differences over all ordered pairs is 800; dividing by 2n² × mean = 2 × 25 × 40 = 2,000 gives 0.40. 0.50 is the top person's income share, 0.20 counts each pair only once (sum 400) but still divides by 2n² × mean, and 0.80 forgets the factor of 2 in the denominator.

questions.q: Which statement about income and wealth inequality in the UK is correct?
options: Wealth is more unequally distributed than income
Income and wealth are both stocks measured at a point in time
The Gini coefficient can only be calculated for wealth
Taxes and benefits have no effect on measured income inequality
questions.why: Wealth (accumulated over lifetimes and inherited) is much more concentrated than income. Income is a flow over a period, not a stock; the Gini can measure any distribution; and comparing market and disposable income shows that taxes and benefits reduce measured income inequality.

questions.q: Explain two causes of rising income inequality in advanced economies since 1980 and evaluate one policy response.
markScheme: Cause 1 explained with mechanism, e.g. skill-biased technological change (Goldin and Katz)
Cause 2 explained, e.g. globalisation/offshoring, decline of unions, top tax cuts, superstar firms, r > g
Policy described (e.g. progressive taxation, minimum wage, education)
Evaluation: benefits vs costs (incentives, evasion, employment effects, time lags)
Judgement linked to the causes identified
questions.modelAnswer: One cause is skill-biased technological change: computers and automation raised the productivity of graduates and replaced many routine middle-skill jobs, so the wage premium for education rose when the supply of graduates did not keep pace, as Goldin and Katz argue. A second is globalisation: trade with lower-wage economies and offshoring reduced demand for less-skilled manufacturing workers in rich countries, while managers and owners of firms with global reach gained. A policy response is expanding education and skills. Because it raises the supply of skilled workers it tackles the first cause directly and changes market incomes rather than relying on redistribution, so it avoids some of Okun's efficiency costs. However, it takes decades to work, its benefits depend on the quality of provision, and it does little for workers already displaced or for wealth concentration at the very top. It is therefore best combined with progressive taxes and benefits in the short run.

questions.q: Output grows 3% a year, capital 4% and labour 1%. With a capital share of 0.3, what is TFP growth?
questions.why: g_A = 3 − 0.3 × 4 − 0.7 × 1 = 3 − 1.2 − 0.7 = 1.1%. 2.0% subtracts unweighted labour growth only, 1.8% subtracts only the capital contribution, and −0.1% swaps the weights, applying 0.7 to capital growth and 0.3 to labour growth (3 − 2.8 − 0.3).

questions.q: In the Solow model, what happens in the long run after a permanent increase in the saving rate?
options: Output per worker rises to a higher level, but its long-run growth rate is unchanged
Output per worker grows permanently faster
Output per worker falls because consumption falls
Nothing, because saving has no effect on capital
questions.why: More saving raises investment, so the economy moves to a higher steady-state capital and output per worker, growing faster only during the transition; diminishing returns stop permanent faster growth. Output per worker does not fall (consumption may or may not rise, depending on the golden rule), and saving does feed investment and capital.

questions.q: Explain why endogenous growth theories were developed in response to the Solow model, and outline one policy implication.
markScheme: Solow: diminishing returns to capital mean long-run growth depends on exogenous technological progress, left unexplained
Endogenous growth explains technology from within: Romer's non-rival ideas and R&D incentives; Aghion-Howitt creative destruction
Increasing returns/spillovers allow sustained growth from investment in knowledge
Policy implication explained, e.g. R&D subsidies, education, patents/competition policy balance
Evaluation or caveat (e.g. inverted-U between competition and innovation, measurement of spillovers)
questions.modelAnswer: In the Solow model capital faces diminishing returns, so accumulating capital cannot sustain growth; long-run growth in income per head comes only from technological progress, which the model assumes rather than explains. Endogenous growth theory tries to explain that progress. Romer (1990) treats ideas as non-rival: once discovered they can be used by everyone, so investment in research creates spillovers and increasing returns, and firms invest because temporary monopoly profits reward innovation. Aghion and Howitt (1992) model growth as Schumpeterian creative destruction, where entrants with better technologies replace incumbents. One implication is that governments can raise long-run growth by supporting research, through R&D tax credits or public science, because private firms capture only part of the social return. Policy must also balance patents, which reward innovators, with competition, which spurs incumbents to innovate; too much protection or too little competition can both slow growth.

questions.q: A bank has assets of £200bn funded by £190bn of deposits and borrowing and £10bn of equity. By what percentage must asset values fall to wipe out its equity?
questions.why: Equity is 10 ÷ 200 = 5% of assets, so a 5% fall in asset values (£10bn) wipes it out. 10% is the equity in £bn mistaken for a percentage, 20% is the leverage multiple, and 95% is the debt share of funding.

questions.q: According to the Diamond-Dybvig model, why can a fundamentally solvent bank suffer a run?
options: Because if depositors expect others to withdraw, it is individually rational to withdraw first, and forced asset sales can make the fear self-fulfilling
Because banks always hold less in assets than they owe depositors
Because deposit insurance encourages depositors to withdraw
Because central banks are legally unable to lend to banks
questions.why: The model has two equilibria: when depositors fear others will withdraw, running first is rational, and selling illiquid assets at a discount can turn a liquidity problem into insolvency. A solvent bank's assets exceed its liabilities by definition; deposit insurance is a remedy that removes the incentive to run; and central banks can lend as lender of last resort.

questions.q: Explain how the post-2008 reforms (higher capital requirements, liquidity rules and ring-fencing) address the causes of the 2007-09 crisis, and identify one remaining weakness.
markScheme: Capital: more loss-absorbing equity reduces leverage and the chance losses cause insolvency; leverage ratio as a backstop
Liquidity rules (LCR) make banks hold liquid assets to survive outflows, addressing runs on wholesale funding (e.g. Northern Rock)
Ring-fencing protects retail deposits and payments from investment-banking losses and eases resolution
Resolution/bail-in reduces too-big-to-fail moral hazard
Weakness identified, e.g. risks migrating to non-banks (LDI 2022), interest-rate risk and fast digital runs (SVB 2023), regulatory arbitrage, procyclicality
questions.modelAnswer: Before 2008 many banks were highly leveraged, so modest losses on mortgage-related assets threatened their solvency. Basel III raised the quantity and quality of capital and added a leverage ratio, so banks can absorb larger losses before failing. Banks such as Northern Rock had also relied on short-term wholesale funding that disappeared; the Liquidity Coverage Ratio requires enough high-quality liquid assets to survive a 30-day stress, reducing run risk. Ring-fencing separates retail deposits and payments from riskier investment banking, so losses in trading cannot directly endanger ordinary savers, and resolution regimes with bail-in debt make it more credible that shareholders and creditors rather than taxpayers bear losses, reducing moral hazard. A remaining weakness is that risk can migrate outside the regulated banking sector: the 2022 LDI episode involved pension funds, not banks, and still required Bank of England intervention. The 2023 failure of Silicon Valley Bank also showed that digitally driven runs can be far faster than regulators had assumed.

questions.q: Demand is P = 100 − Q and marginal cost is constant at 20. What is the deadweight loss under monopoly compared with perfect competition?
questions.why: Competition gives Q = 80, P = 20; monopoly sets MR = 100 − 2Q = 20, so Q = 40 and P = 60. The deadweight loss triangle is ½ × 40 × 40 = 800. 1,600 is the monopoly profit, 3,200 is consumer surplus under competition, and 400 halves the triangle a second time.

questions.q: Four firms have market shares of 40%, 30%, 20% and 10%. What is the HHI?
questions.why: HHI = 40² + 30² + 20² + 10² = 1,600 + 900 + 400 + 100 = 3,000. 100 is the sum of the shares, 10,000 is the value for a pure monopoly, and 2,500 is the HHI for four equal firms of 25% each.

questions.q: Rising markups have been interpreted as evidence of declining competition. Outline the evidence and evaluate this interpretation.
markScheme: Evidence: De Loecker, Eeckhout and Unger (2020) aggregate markups rose from 21% to 61% over marginal cost (US listed firms, 1980 to 2016), median unchanged, driven by top firms; rising concentration and superstar firms (Autor et al.)
Interpretation 1: weaker competition (mergers, network effects, barriers to entry) leading to higher prices and deadweight loss
Alternative: higher fixed or intangible costs (R&D, software) mean markups over marginal cost are needed to cover them; superstar firms may be more productive
Measurement issues in estimating marginal cost; listed-firm samples
Judgement and policy implication (e.g. focus on entry barriers, merger control, digital regulation)
questions.modelAnswer: De Loecker, Eeckhout and Unger (2020) estimate that the average markup of price over marginal cost for US listed firms rose from 21% in 1980 to 61% by 2016 (an aggregate, sales-weighted measure), while the median markup was unchanged, so the rise was concentrated among the highest-markup firms. Autor and co-authors find that many industries have become more concentrated around a few 'superstar' firms. One reading is that competition has weakened through mergers, network effects and barriers to entry, letting firms raise prices and restrict output, which would reduce welfare and shift income from workers to owners. But high markups over marginal cost are not proof of harm: firms with large fixed costs in software, R&D or brands must price above marginal cost to cover them, and superstar firms may dominate because they are more productive and have passed lower costs on to consumers. Estimating marginal cost is also difficult and listed firms are not the whole economy. My judgement is that the evidence justifies closer scrutiny of mergers and of digital markets with tipping dynamics, as the UK's 2024 digital markets law allows, rather than treating size alone as a problem.

questions.q: "A carbon price is all that is needed to tackle climate change." Discuss.
markScheme: Explains climate change as a negative externality and global public good; MSC > MPC; over-production and deadweight loss (diagram)
Pigouvian logic: carbon price internalises the externality; tax vs cap-and-trade; cost-effectiveness via equal marginal abatement costs
Limits 1: global free-riding and carbon leakage; need for international agreements (Paris 2015) or border adjustments
Limits 2: other market failures: innovation spillovers (R&D under-provided), network/infrastructure coordination, information failures, credit constraints
Limits 3: distributional effects (regressive energy costs) and political feasibility; revenue recycling
Discounting and uncertainty (Stern vs Nordhaus; Weitzman prices vs quantities) affect the level of the price
Evidence/examples: EU ETS, UK ETS, UK Climate Change Act carbon budgets
Reasoned conclusion: carbon pricing is central but not sufficient; complementary policies needed
questions.modelAnswer:
Climate change is a negative externality: those who emit greenhouse gases do not bear the damage they cause, which falls on others worldwide and on future generations. The social marginal cost of fossil-fuel use exceeds the private marginal cost, so markets produce too many emissions and there is a deadweight loss. Pigou's solution is to price the externality. A carbon price equal to the marginal damage at the optimum makes emitters internalise the cost, and because every firm faces the same price, each abates until its marginal abatement cost equals that price, so a given reduction is achieved at least total cost. This is the main argument for carbon pricing and why the EU and UK operate emissions trading schemes.

However, carbon pricing alone faces several limits. First, the climate is a global public good. A price in one country cuts only that country's emissions, and others have an incentive to free-ride; production may also relocate to countries without carbon pricing (leakage). This is why the Paris Agreement of 2015 relies on nationally determined contributions and why border carbon adjustments are being introduced, but neither solves free-riding fully.

Second, there are additional market failures. Clean-technology research creates knowledge spillovers that private firms cannot capture, so even with a correct carbon price, innovation will be under-provided; endogenous growth theory supports R&D subsidies. Networks such as electricity grids and charging points involve coordination problems and large fixed costs, and households may lack information or access to credit for insulation or heat pumps. Regulations, standards and public investment can address these where prices alone respond weakly.

Third, setting the price is hard. The social cost of carbon depends heavily on the discount rate: Stern's low rate implies urgent, expensive action, while Nordhaus's market-based rate supports a gradual ramp. Under uncertainty, Weitzman's analysis shows a tax and a cap are not equivalent, and the UK's legally binding carbon budgets under the Climate Change Act 2008 arguably favour quantity certainty.

Finally, carbon prices are regressive because poorer households spend a larger share of income on energy, and they can be politically fragile, as protests against fuel taxes in several countries have shown. Revenue can be recycled as dividends or targeted support, but this must be designed in.

In conclusion, a carbon price is the most efficient core instrument because it harnesses decentralised information about abatement costs. But it is not all that is needed: international cooperation, innovation support, infrastructure investment, targeted regulation and compensation for losers are all required to reach net zero at acceptable cost.

questions.q:
(a) An economy's expectations-augmented Phillips curve is π = πᵉ − 0.5(u − 5), with inflation and unemployment in %. Expected inflation is 2% and unemployment is 4%. Calculate inflation. If expectations then adjust fully to this inflation rate and unemployment stays at 4%, what is inflation next period? [5]
(b) The central bank follows i = 1 + π + 0.5(π − 2) + 0.5x, where x is the output gap (%). Calculate the policy rate when inflation is 4% and the output gap is +1%, and the real interest rate implied. [5]
(c) Using your answers and the UK's experience since 2021, discuss why expectations matter for the cost of reducing inflation. [10]
markScheme: (a) With πᵉ = 2.5%, π = 2.5 + 0.5 = 3%: inflation accelerates while u < u* = 5%
(b) Real rate ≈ 6.5 − 4 = 2.5% (exactly about 2.4%); positive real rate shows policy is tight; rate rises more than one-for-one with inflation
(c) Expectations determine the position of the short-run Phillips curve; anchored expectations mean less unemployment needed (sacrifice ratio lower)
(c) Credibility from independence (1997) and the 2% target; second-round effects from wages and price-setting
(c) UK evidence: energy and post-pandemic shocks, CPI peak 11.1% (Oct 2022), Bank Rate raised from 0.1% to 5.25%; concerns about wage growth and de-anchoring
(c) Balanced conclusion: supply shocks vs demand; risks of over- and under-tightening; lags
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) π = 2 − 0.5 × (4 − 5) = 2 + 0.5 = 2.5%. Unemployment is one point below the natural rate of 5%, so inflation exceeds expectations by 0.5 points. If expectations adjust to 2.5% and unemployment stays at 4%, next period π = 2.5 + 0.5 = 3%. Holding unemployment below its natural rate makes inflation rise by 0.5 points each period: it accelerates rather than settling at a higher level.

(b) i = 1 + 4 + 0.5 × (4 − 2) + 0.5 × 1 = 1 + 4 + 1 + 0.5 = 6.5%. The real interest rate is approximately 6.5 − 4 = 2.5% (exactly 1.065/1.04 − 1 ≈ 2.4%). Because the policy rate rises by 1.5 points for each 1-point rise in inflation, the real rate rises when inflation rises, so policy tightens in real terms, which is necessary to stabilise inflation.

(c) Part (a) shows that expectations shift the short-run Phillips curve. Once people expect higher inflation, the economy can only get back to low inflation by holding unemployment above the natural rate long enough for expectations to fall. The more firmly expectations are anchored at the target, the smaller this cost (the sacrifice ratio), because people expect inflation to come back down and set wages and prices accordingly.

The UK's experience illustrates this. After the pandemic, supply bottlenecks, a tight labour market and the energy price shock following Russia's invasion of Ukraine pushed CPI inflation to 11.1% in October 2022. Much of this was a cost-push shock that monetary policy cannot reverse directly. The MPC's concern was second-round effects: if workers and firms came to expect persistently high inflation, wage settlements and price-setting would keep inflation high after energy prices fell. The Bank therefore raised Bank Rate from 0.1% (starting in December 2021) to 5.25% by August 2023. In terms of part (b), it sought positive real rates to signal commitment and keep expectations anchored. Inflation fell back to around the 2% target by mid-2024, without the very large rise in unemployment of earlier disinflations, which supports the view that credibility, built up since independence in 1997, reduced the cost. However, inflation rose again in 2025, and services inflation and wage growth proved persistent, suggesting expectations were not perfectly anchored.

There are caveats. Critics argue the Bank was slow to tighten in 2021 because it judged inflation to be transitory, which risked damaging credibility; others argue that because the shock came from supply, over-tightening imposed unnecessary costs given long policy lags. Overall, expectations matter because they decide whether a temporary shock becomes persistent inflation, and a credible commitment to the target is what keeps the cost of bringing inflation down low.
